s:
Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church
Þæt sǣd þe fēoll bē ðām weġe mid twyfealdre dare losode, ðāðā weġferende hit fortrǣdon, and fugelas tōbǣron.
The seed that fell by the way perished to a double injury, when the wayfarer tread upon it and when the birds carried it away.
Ne mæġ him þonne sē flǣsċhoma, þonne him þæt feorg losað, ne swēte forswelgan, ne sār ġefēlan, ne hond onhrēran ne mid hyġe þenċan.
Then the fleshen-body cannot do anything for him, when life comes to nothing for him, nor swallow sweet, nor feel sorrow, nor move hand, nor think with wit.
y: Related to lēosan (“to lose”). Compare los (“loss”).
From Proto-West Germanic *luhs. Cognate with Old Saxon lohs, Old High German luhs, Old Swedish lō. See los.

s: Lot (nephew of Abraham in the Bible)

early 12th century, in the Peterborough Chronicle
...ut of Scotlande into Loðene on Englaland...
...out of Scotland into Lothian in England...
...⁊ se b[iscop] of Loþene I[ohan]...
...and the bishop of Lothian Iohan...
y:
Potentially from Proto-Brythonic *Lugudūniānā, or Proto-Celtic *lutā.
According to A. D. Mills, in A Dictionary of British Place Names, named after "one Leudonus".
See etymology of Lothian on Wikipedia for more information.

From Proto-West Germanic *luþō, from Proto-Germanic *luþô (“coarse woolen cloth”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lūt-, *lūd- (“weak, languid”). Cognate with Old Frisian lotha (“thick robe”), Old Saxon lotho (“thick wool robe”), Old High German lodo, ludo (“thick woolen cloth”).
From Proto-West Germanic *lubistikō, *lubistik, from Latin levisticum (“lovage”), with folk-etymological alteration after lufu (“love”) and stiċe (“stitch”): literally “love-stitch”.

s: Ġif þū wille bēon ġelufod, lufa.
If you want to be loved, love.

c. 992, Ælfric, "The Second Sunday After Easter"
Sē Hǣlend cwæþ be him, "Iċ eom gōd hierde, and iċ oncnāwe mīn sċēap, and hīe oncnāwaþ mē." Þæt is, "Iċ lufiġe hīe, and hīe lufiaþ mē."
Jesus said about himself, "I'm a good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and they know me." That is, "I love them, and they love me."
When you pray, don't be like hypocrites. They love to pray standing in synagogues and on street corners so that people will see them.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *lubōn, derived from the noun *lubu (“love”). Equivalent to lufu + -ian. Cognate with Old Frisian luvia, Old High German lubōn.

s:
late 10th century, Ælfric, "Saint Agnes, Virgin"
Iċ hæbbe ōðerne lufiend...

c. 995, Ælfric, Extracts on Grammar in English
Amans Deum (“lufiende God”) is dǣlnimend, and amans Deī (“Godes lufiend”) is nama.
Amans Deum (“loving God“) is a participle, and amans Deī (“God's lover“) is a noun.

y: Probably an alteration of older lēoflīċ. Equivalent to lufu + -līċ.

s: amiable and kind to the men that are dear to him
y: From lufu + -sum. Piecewise doublet of lofsum.

s: Sēo sōðe lufu nǣfre ne ātēoraþ.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *lubu, from Proto-Germanic *lubō. Cognate with Old Frisian luve, Old High German luba, Gothic *𐌻𐌿𐌱𐍉 (*lubō).

Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
Þā æfter him feng Mellitus to erċebisċopdōme þe ǣr wæs bisċop on Lundene...Ðā æfter feng tō þām erċebisċopdōme Iūstus...
Then after him Mellitus, who was previously bishop of London, ascended to the archbishopdom..then afterwards Justus ascended to the archbishopdom.

late 10th century, Ælfric, "Sermon on the Efficacy of the Holy Mass"
Sē ealdormann sealde hine sumum Frīsan of Lundene.
The aldorman sold him to a Frisian from London.
y: Together with Middle Welsh Llundein cannot be directly from Latin Londinium, which would yield *Lynden via i-mutation. But both may continue Vulgar Latin *Lundeinju (Late British Latin) if the medial -i- of the original word was short.

s:
Laws of the Anglo-Saxons: Eadmund I
Ēadmund cyngc ġesamnode miċelne sinoð tō Lundenbyriġ on ðā hālgan ēasterlīcan tīd æġðer ġe godcundra ġe worldcundra: ðǣr wæs Ōda arċebisċop ⁊ Wulfstān arċebisċop ⁊ maneġa ōðre bisċopas smeagende ymbon heora sāwle rǣd ⁊ þāra þe him underþēodde wǣron.

King Edmund assembled a great synod in London during the holy Eastertide of men both godly and worldly: there was Archbishop Oda and Archbishop Wulfstan, and many other bishops under them considering the welfare of their souls.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
Þȳ ilcan ġēare forbarn Lundenbyriġ, ⁊ on þām ilcan ġēare forðferdon tweġen ealdormenn, Æþelmǣr on Hāmtūnsċīre ⁊ Ēadwine on Sūþseaxum. ⁊ Æþelmǣres līc līð on Wintanċeastre on nīwan mynstre, ⁊ Ēadwines on þām mynstre æt Abbandūne. Þǣs ilcan ġēare forðferdon twā abbodessan on Dorsǣtum, Herelufu on Sċeaftesbyriġ ⁊ Wulfwin on Werhām.

In the same year [982], London burned down, and in the same year, two princes passed away: Ethelmer in Hamptonshire and Edwin in Sussex. Ethemer's body lies in the new monastery in Winchester, and Edwin's in the monastery at Abingdon. In the same year, two abbesses passed away in Dorset: Herelufu in Shaftesbury and Wulfwin in Wareham.

y: Literally, “London's bridge”, or more loosely translated as “the bridge of London”.

s: upp and niðer on þā Lundenescan strǣta
up and down the London streets

c. 995, Ælfric, Extracts on Grammar in English
Sume naman ġeswutoliaþ þæs mannes ēðel: rōmānus ("Rōmānisċ"), londiniēnsis ("Lundenisċ"), wiltuniēnsis ("Wiltūnisċ").
Some nouns tell you a person's hometown: rōmānus (“Roman”), londiniēnsis (“Londoner”), wiltuniēnsis (“Wiltonian”).

Laws of Hlothhere and Eadric
Ġif Cantwara æniġ in Lundenwīc fēoh ġebyċġe, hæbbe him tweġen oððe ðrēo unfācne ċeorlas tō ġewitnesse oþþe cyninges wīcġerēfan.
If any person of Kent buys property in London, he should have two or three trustworthy men or the king's reeve, as a witness.

y: From Proto-West Germanic *lundulagō, equivalent to *lund (“loin, fat”) + *laga (“lier, that which is fixed”). Cognate with Old Frisian lundlaga (“kidney”).

From Proto-Germanic *lunganjō, an extension of Proto-Germanic *lungô, from Proto-Indo-European *lengʷʰ- (“light, agile, nimble”). Cognate with Old Frisian lungen, Old Saxon lungannia, Old High German lunganna.
From Proto-West Germanic *lungr, from Proto-Germanic *lungraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ln̥gʷʰrós (“lightweight”).
From Proto-West Germanic *lūs. Compare Old High German lūs, Old Norse lús.

s: Him wæs metes micel lust ― he had a craving for food. (Ælfric's Homilies)

Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church
Woruldcara, and welan, and flǣsċlīċe lustas forsmoriað ðǣs mōdes ðrotan, and ne geðafiað gōdne willan infaran tō his heortan, swilċe hī ðone līflīċan blǣd forðrǣstne ācwellon. Twā wiðerrǣde ðing geðēodde Drihten on ðisum cwyde, þæt sind ymhīdiġnyssa and lustas.

Concern about worldly things, and wealth, and carnal lusts choke the throat of the mind, and do not allow good desires into the heart, as if they killed it by crushing the living fruit. The Lord connected two contrary things in this saying, which are cares and lusts.

c. 1000, Ælfric of Eynsham, "Genesis;" reprinted and normalized in Bruce Mitchell, Fred C. Robinson, A Guide to Old English, Fifth Edition, Oxford.: Blackwell Publishers Ltd, 1992, reprinted in 1999, Part II, Section 2, page 174, lines 11-13
Then saw the woman that the tree was good to eat, as she thought, and beautiful to the eyes and desirable in sight;
strong accusative masculine singular of lustbǣre
strong genitive/dative/instrumental feminine singular of lustbǣre
with joy or pleasure, joyfully, gladly, with lust

y: Uncertain. Apparently from *lust + *moce. The first element may be lust (“pleasure”) or may refer to a different unknown term. The second element is probably related to *moc (“dung, muck”) (found in hlōsmoc (“pigsty dung”)), distantly related to Old Norse myki (“manure, dung”), whence Middle English muk, mok (“dung, filth”), English muck.
From Proto-West Germanic *lustusam, from Proto-Germanic *lustusamaz, equivalent to lust + -sum.

s:
late 9th century, translation of Orosius’ History Against the Pagans
...and ðā syndon swȳþe fæġere and lustsumlīce on tō sēonne...
...and those are very beautiful and pleasant to look at...

y: By surface analysis, lust (“desire, pleasure, lust”) + wine (“friend”).

y: From Proto-West Germanic *lubi, from Proto-Germanic *lubją (“herb, poison, love potion”). Akin to Old High German luppi, Old Norse lyf.
From Proto-West Germanic *lubisnu, from Proto-Germanic *lubisnō, from *lubją + *-snō. Equivalent to lybb (“drug, medicine, poison”) + -sn.

y: From Proto-West Germanic *lubittjan, *lobattjan, equivalent to lof + -ettan. Alternatively, from Proto-West Germanic *lubbjattjan (“to drug, charm”), equivalent to lybb + -ettan.

s:
late 10th century, Ælfric, On the Seasons of the Year
Nis nā sēo orðung þe wē ūt blāwaþ and inn ātēoþ ūru sāwol, ac is sēo lyft þe wē on libbaþ on þissum dēadlīcan līfe.
The breath that we draw in and blow out is not our soul, but the air that we live in during this mortal life.

c. 992, Ælfric, "The Exaltation of the Holy Cross"
Wynsum brǣþ āfylde þā lyft.
A pleasant aroma filled the air.

late 10th century, Ælfric, On the Seasons of the Year
Hæġl cymþ of reġndropum þonne hīe bēoþ ġefrorene uppe on þǣre lyfte, and swā siþþan feallaþ.
Hail comes from raindrops when they are frozen up in the atmosphere, and so fall to the ground.

c. 992, Ælfric, "St. Benedict, Abbot"
And wæs þā swā stille weder þæt nān wolcn næs on þǣre lyfte ġesewen.
And the weather was so calm that there wasn't a cloud in the sky.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *lufti, possibly rebuilt from the plural or remodelled as a ti-stem from *luftu, from Proto-Germanic *luftuz. Doublet of loft.
From Proto-West Germanic *lugi. Cognate with Old Saxon luggi (“lying”), Old High German lucki (“lying”).
From Proto-West Germanic *lugin, from Proto-Germanic *luginaz (“lying”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to tell lies, swear, bemoan”).

From Proto-West Germanic *luginu, from Proto-Germanic *luginō, *lugį̄ (“lie, falsehood”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to tell lies, swear, bemoan”). Cognate with Old Saxon lugina (“falsehood”), Danish løgn (“lie”), Norwegian lygn (“lie”). More at lie.
